source: Katzung16 ch1, ch36, ch55; KDT8 ch64-65

cards.front: What is a biologic drug?
cards.back: A large-molecule therapeutic, usually a protein (hormone, cytokine, monoclonal antibody, fusion protein), often made by recombinant DNA technology in living cells rather than by chemical synthesis. Oligonucleotide drugs are also grouped with biopharmaceuticals, although some (e.g. antisense oligonucleotides) are made synthetically, so the biological/small-molecule boundary is not sharp.

cards.front: Complete: half-life of IgG-based biologics
cards.text: IgG-based biologics persist in plasma because the {{neonatal Fc receptor (FcRn)}} recycles them and rescues them from {{lysosomal}} degradation; rituximab has a half-life of about {{22 days}}.

cards.front: How are monoclonal antibodies named, and what change did WHO make in 2021?
cards.back: Names end in -mab. The syllable before it shows origin: -omab mouse (murine), -ximab chimeric (human constant Fc fused to mouse variable Fv domains), -zumab humanised (only the antigen-binding CDRs are non-human, inserted into a human IgG scaffold), -umab fully human (from transgenic mice carrying human Ig genes, or phage display). Another syllable can show function, e.g. -li- immunomodulatory (nivolumab, cemiplimab). Examples: cetuximab, trastuzumab, bevacizumab. In October 2021 WHO changed the scheme for newly named antibodies: the single -mab stem is being replaced by four distinct stems that describe the antibody's composition; names assigned up to 2021 keep the old pattern.

cards.front: Why do monoclonal antibody names end in -mab, and what does the syllable just before it tell you?
cards.back: The stem -mab marks a monoclonal antibody. The infix before it shows origin: -momab mouse, -ximab chimeric, -zumab humanised, -umab human.

cards.front: Complete: antibody name origin stems
cards.text: Cetuximab is {{chimeric}} (-ximab), trastuzumab is {{humanised}} (-zumab), and names ending {{-umab}} are fully human.

cards.front: Short note: Humanisation of monoclonal antibodies

points: Murine antibodies trigger human anti-mouse antibodies (HAMA)
HAMA clear the drug very quickly
Murine: whole mouse antibody
Chimeric: mouse variable regions, human constant regions
Humanised: only the antigen-binding CDRs are murine
Fully human: transgenic mice with human Ig loci, or phage display
Lower antigenicity and a longer half-life
Cetuximab (chimeric) still provokes HAMA in about 4% of patients
Fab fragments (e.g. arcitumomab) are less immunogenic than intact murine antibodies

cards.front: How long does rituximab stay in plasma, and what does that mean for dosing?
cards.back: Half-life about 22 days, so it is given weekly for 4 weeks, then as maintenance every 3 to 6 months (GG14 ch72).

cards.front: Why does a chimeric antibody such as cetuximab still cause anti-drug antibodies, and how does humanisation help?
cards.back: Chimeric antibodies keep mouse variable regions, which the immune system can recognise as foreign. Humanised antibodies keep only the mouse CDRs, so immunogenicity falls; fully human antibodies reduce it further.

cards.front: Essay: Biologics versus small-molecule drugs

points: Large proteins, antibodies or oligonucleotides versus small chemical drugs
Mostly produced by recombinant DNA technology in living cells
Given parenterally; most need injection or infusion
Broken down by proteolysis in lysosomes rather than by CYP enzymes
IgG-based products stay in plasma for a long time because FcRn recycles them (rituximab half-life about 22 days)
Target-mediated uptake and catabolism can add to clearance
High specificity for a single target, often extracellular (cytokines, receptors, cell-surface antigens)
Dose-response can be bell-shaped or U-shaped
Immunogenicity with anti-drug antibodies (e.g. HAMA)
Infusion reactions and cytokine release syndrome
Target-related immunosuppression and infection risk
Biosimilars: copies of large proteins cannot be shown identical, so approval needs analytical, animal and clinical comparison

cards.front: Ligand blockade versus receptor blockade: how do they differ, with one example each?
cards.back: Ligand blockade: the antibody binds the soluble ligand so it cannot reach its receptor (bevacizumab binds VEGF-A; anti-TNF antibodies neutralise TNF-alpha). Receptor blockade: the antibody binds the receptor's extracellular domain and prevents ligand binding (trastuzumab on HER2, cetuximab on EGFR).

cards.front: What is antibody-dependent cell-mediated cytotoxicity (ADCC), and which cells mediate it?
cards.back: The antibody's Fc region engages Fc receptors on NK cells or phagocytes, which then kill the antibody-coated target cell. IgG1 interacts with Fc receptors more strongly than IgG2 or IgG4, and Fc engineering can enhance or suppress ADCC. Examples: elotuzumab (SLAMF7 on myeloma cells); rituximab, ofatumumab and obinutuzumab (CD20, together with complement-dependent lysis).

cards.front: What is complement-dependent cytotoxicity (CDC), and which antibody shows it?
cards.back: Antibody bound to the target cell activates complement; the membrane attack complex (C5b to C9) then lyses the cell. IgG1 activates complement better than IgG2 or IgG4. Rituximab (anti-CD20) kills B cells mostly by CDC and ADCC; daratumumab (anti-CD38) may kill myeloma cells by CDC, ADCC or apoptosis.

cards.front: Complete: immune checkpoint targets
cards.text: Ipilimumab blocks {{CTLA-4}}, nivolumab and pembrolizumab block {{PD-1}}, and atezolizumab blocks {{PD-L1}}. Blocking these brakes releases antitumour T cells.

cards.front: Name the antibody targets: rituximab, trastuzumab, bevacizumab, cetuximab.
cards.back: Rituximab: CD20 on B cells. Trastuzumab: HER2 receptor. Bevacizumab: VEGF-A ligand. Cetuximab: EGF receptor. Bevacizumab is ligand blockade; the others hit a cell-surface antigen or receptor.

cards.front: What is a bispecific T-cell engager (BiTE)? Give one example and its main toxicities.
cards.back: A bispecific antibody with one arm binding a tumour antigen and the other binding CD3 on T cells, bringing T cells close to tumour cells so they kill them. Blinatumomab (CD19 x CD3) is used in relapsed or refractory B-cell precursor ALL and in ALL with minimal residual disease; teclistamab (BCMA x CD3) in multiple myeloma. Monitor for cytokine release syndrome, neurological toxicity and infections.

cards.front: Short note: Rituximab

points: Chimeric murine/human anti-CD20 IgG1 on B lymphocytes
Kills mainly by complement-dependent cytotoxicity and ADCC; also apoptosis
B cells depleted within 3 weeks; recovery by about 12 months
CD20-positive non-Hodgkin lymphoma, alone or with chemotherapy
CLL with chemotherapy
Rheumatoid arthritis with methotrexate
GPA and microscopic polyangiitis with glucocorticoids
Also used in pemphigus vulgaris and refractory lupus nephritis
Infusion reactions: slow infusion rate; pretreat with antihistamines and corticosteroids
Tumour lysis syndrome when many circulating tumour cells
Hepatitis B reactivation; rarely PML from JC virus
Severe mucocutaneous reactions including SJS
Hypogammaglobulinaemia and delayed autoimmune cytopenias

cards.front: Why can an anti-PD-1 or anti-CTLA-4 antibody treat cancer, and what toxicity pattern follows?
cards.back: They block inhibitory T-cell checkpoints (CTLA-4, PD-1 or PD-L1), releasing antitumour T cells against the tumour.

cards.front: Short note: Monoclonal antibodies in therapeutics

points: Trastuzumab: humanised antibody that binds and blocks the HER2 receptor
Cetuximab: chimeric antibody against the EGF receptor, blocks signalling
Rituximab: anti-CD20 antibody that depletes B lymphocytes, used in B-cell lymphomas
Infliximab and adalimumab neutralise TNF; used in rheumatoid arthritis
Rituximab combined with methotrexate in rheumatoid arthritis
Omalizumab: anti-IgE antibody for asthma; neutralises free IgE
Erenumab: fully human antibody to the CGRP receptor, for migraine prevention
Muromonab-CD3: murine antibody to CD3 on T cells, the oldest of this type
Daclizumab: humanised anti-CD25 that blocks the IL-2 receptor; combined with glucocorticoids and calcineurin antagonists
Denosumab: anti-RANKL antibody that blocks osteoclast proliferation and differentiation
Idarucizumab: reversal agent for dabigatran
Abciximab: Fab fragment against GP IIb/IIIa, an antiplatelet
Infusion reactions, e.g. fever, chills, urticaria and bronchospasm with infliximab

cards.front: Compare how rituximab, checkpoint inhibitors and blinatumomab each recruit the immune system against cancer.
cards.back: Rituximab: Fc-mediated killing of CD20 cells by CDC and ADCC. Checkpoint inhibitors (ipilimumab, nivolumab, pembrolizumab, atezolizumab): free T cells by blocking CTLA-4, PD-1 or PD-L1. Blinatumomab (CD19 x CD3): links a T cell to the B-cell target.

points: Antibodies hit a defined target on tumour or immune cells; names show origin (-xi chimeric, -zu humanised, -u human)
Rituximab (CD20, ADCC and CDC)

Bevacizumab (VEGF-A)

cards.front: What is an antibody-drug conjugate (ADC), and how is its payload released?
cards.back: A monoclonal antibody chemically linked to a cytotoxic payload (toxin or drug; radionuclides are used similarly). The antibody binds its tumour antigen, the complex is internalised, and the payload is released inside the cell by proteolytic cleavage. Payloads include microtubule disruptors (emtansine, MMAE) and topoisomerase inhibitors (deruxtecan).

cards.front: Complete: antibody-drug conjugate payloads
cards.text: Emtansine and MMAE are {{microtubule}} disruptors, whereas deruxtecan is a {{topoisomerase}} inhibitor; the payload is released inside the cell after the antibody is internalised.

cards.front: What is the advantage of linking a toxin to an antibody rather than giving the toxin alone?
cards.back: The antibody delivers the payload to cells carrying the tumour antigen; after internalisation the payload is released inside the cell, aiming the cytotoxic drug at the target.

cards.front: Which fusion proteins carry an IgG Fc, and what does each bind?
cards.back: Etanercept: two TNF p75 receptor domains, binds TNF-alpha and lymphotoxin. Abatacept and belatacept: CTLA-4 extracellular domain, bind CD80/86 and block CD28 co-stimulation.

cards.front: Trastuzumab emtansine: target, payload and key toxicity
cards.back: Anti-HER2 antibody linked to mertansine (emtansine), a microtubule disruptor. Used in HER2-positive breast cancer that recurred or progressed after trastuzumab and a taxane. Its toxicities include those of trastuzumab plus hepatotoxicity from the payload.

cards.front: Brentuximab vedotin: target, payload and main indications
cards.back: Chimeric anti-CD30 IgG1 linked to monomethyl auristatin E (MMAE), a microtubule disruptor released inside the cell by proteolytic cleavage. Used in Hodgkin lymphoma after failed autologous stem cell transplant or after at least two prior regimens, and in systemic anaplastic large cell lymphoma after at least one prior multiagent regimen. Monitor mainly for neutropenia and peripheral sensory neuropathy.

cards.front: Short note: Fusion proteins in immunology (etanercept and abatacept)

points: Etanercept: two soluble TNF p75 receptor domains linked to the Fc of human IgG1
Abatacept and belatacept: extracellular domain of CTLA-4 fused to the Fc of human IgG1
Etanercept binds TNF-alpha and also inhibits lymphotoxin (TNF-beta)
Abatacept and belatacept bind CD80/86 and block the CD28 co-stimulatory signal to T cells
Etanercept: rheumatoid arthritis and related arthritides
Abatacept: rheumatoid and other forms of arthritis
Belatacept: prevention of kidney transplant rejection
Infection and TB reactivation risk with TNF blockade
No live vaccines during anti-TNF therapy

cards.front: Short note: Biologic response modifiers and biologic DMARDs

points: Adalimumab, certolizumab pegol, etanercept, golimumab, infliximab
Tocilizumab (IL-6 receptor)
Abatacept (CTLA-4 Fc fusion)
Rituximab (anti-CD20)

No live vaccines
Lymphoma risk

cards.front: Short note: antibody-drug conjugates versus naked antibodies versus fusion proteins

points: Acts by blockade, ADCC or CDC (trastuzumab, rituximab)
Antibody plus cytotoxic payload, released inside the cell after internalisation (trastuzumab emtansine, brentuximab vedotin)
Receptor or ligand domain fused to IgG1 Fc (etanercept, abatacept, belatacept) to trap a cytokine or block co-stimulation
Brentuximab vedotin: CD30 lymphomas; trastuzumab emtansine: HER2 breast cancer; belatacept: kidney transplant

cards.front: What is cytokine release syndrome (CRS), which biologics cause it, and how is it treated?
cards.back: A systemic reaction to a large release of cytokines (TNF, interleukins including IL-6, interferons). Features: fever, chills, rigors, nausea, headache, tachycardia, hypotension, dyspnoea and wheezing; can be life-threatening. Seen with CAR T cells, bispecific T-cell engagers (blinatumomab), immune checkpoint inhibitors, and the first doses of muromonab-CD3. Management: tocilizumab (anti-IL-6 receptor) with or without corticosteroids; corticosteroid pretreatment attenuates the muromonab reaction.

cards.front: Complete: premedication for infusion reactions
cards.text: Infusion reactions to rituximab are dampened by pre-treatment with {{antihistamines}} and {{corticosteroids}}, and by a {{slow infusion rate}}.

cards.front: Which premedication reduces rituximab infusion reactions?
cards.back: Antihistamines before the infusion and a slower infusion rate; reactions are usually mild with pretreatment (GG14 ch72).

cards.front: Which infections must be excluded or watched for with TNF-alpha blockers?
cards.back: Reactivation of latent tuberculosis and valley fever; patients taking TNF blockers should be monitored for past infection.

cards.front: Name the characteristic adverse effect of bevacizumab and trastuzumab.
cards.back: Bevacizumab: haemorrhage, GI perforation, poor wound healing. Trastuzumab: cardiomyopathy.

cards.front: Short note: Infection and malignancy risk with TNF-alpha blockers

points: Adalimumab, certolizumab pegol, etanercept, golimumab, infliximab
Reactivation of tuberculosis
Valley fever (coccidioidomycosis)
Recurrence of past infections
Lymphoma
Live vaccines must not be given during therapy
Check history of past infection and TB before and during treatment

cards.front: A patient on rituximab develops jaundice and rising transaminases. What should you consider?
cards.back: Hepatitis B reactivation, a known risk of rituximab; PML from JC virus is a rare infection risk (GG14 ch72).

cards.front: Essay: Adverse effects of therapeutic monoclonal antibodies

points: Fever, chills, urticaria, mild hypotension; serious hypersensitivity if infused too fast
Premedication and slow increase in infusion rate
With CAR T cells, BiTEs, checkpoint inhibitors and first doses of muromonab-CD3
Tocilizumab with or without corticosteroids
Anti-drug antibodies (HAMA) speed clearance and reduce efficacy
Chimeric and humanised designs lower the risk
B-cell depletion: hypogammaglobulinaemia, hepatitis B reactivation, PML (rituximab)
TB and valley fever reactivation with TNF blockade; no live vaccines
Bevacizumab: haemorrhage, GI perforation, poor wound healing
Trastuzumab: cardiomyopathy
Belantamab mafodotin: ocular (corneal) toxicity
Necitumumab: hypomagnesaemia

cards.front: What is a biosimilar?
cards.back: A biological product that is highly similar to an approved reference product despite minor differences in clinically inactive components, with no clinically meaningful differences in safety, purity and potency. Because proteins come from living cells, differences in glycosylation or conformation can alter PK, PD and immunogenicity, so a biosimilar cannot simply be shown identical like a small-molecule generic. Rang and Dale also contrast biosimilars with 'biobetters' (similar function, superior pharmacology or toxicity).

cards.front: Complete: interchangeable biosimilar insulin
cards.text: Semglee and Rezvoglar are {{interchangeable}} biosimilar insulins with the reference product {{Lantus}} (insulin {{glargine}}).

cards.front: Why can a biosimilar not be approved like a small-molecule generic?
cards.back: A protein made in living cells cannot be shown identical to the reference product; differences in glycosylation or conformation can change PK, PD and immunogenicity, so equivalence must be shown.

cards.front: What must be shown for a biosimilar against its reference product?
cards.back: Therapeutic equivalence must be demonstrated rather than assumed, because glycosylation or conformation differences can change PK, PD and immunogenicity (GG14 ch1).

cards.front: Short note: Biosimilar approval pathway

points: Biologics Price Competition and Innovation Act, enacted with the Affordable Care Act, created an abbreviated licensure pathway for 'similar' biological products
Analytical studies comparing structure and function
Animal studies
One or more clinical studies
Highly similar to the reference product
No clinically meaningful differences in safety, purity and potency
Interpretation of the requirements is still debated; firm rules are unlikely

cards.front: Name two insulin glargine products listed in Katzung besides Lantus.
cards.back: Basaglar and Rezvoglar, listed with Lantus and Toujeo as insulin glargine products.

cards.front: Short note: why biosimilars need a different approval route from generics

points: Large proteins are made in living cells and cannot be proven identical
Differences in glycosylation or conformation can alter PK, PD and immunogenicity
Equivalence to the reference product must be demonstrated
Insulin glargine products such as Basaglar and Rezvoglar

cards.front: What are the main viral vectors used in gene therapy, and which one is used to make CAR-T cells?
cards.back: Retroviruses (including lentivirus) integrate into host DNA, giving permanent expression passed to daughter cells, but random insertion can disrupt genes; a lentiviral vector is used to transduce T cells when making CAR T cells. Adenovirus is highly infective but immunogenic, with transient expression needing repeated doses. Adeno-associated virus is less immunogenic but hard to mass-produce and cannot carry large genes. Non-viral options (liposomes, DNA cassettes) are safer but less efficient.

cards.front: Complete: antisense oligonucleotides (ASO)
cards.text: Antisense oligonucleotides are short single-stranded nucleic-acid chains that bind complementary {{mRNA}} and promote its breakdown by {{ribonuclease H}}. An apolipoprotein C-III antisense (volanesorsen) is available in Europe for severe chylomicronaemia.

cards.front: How do mRNA vaccines work?
cards.back: They deliver messenger RNA encoding an antigen, packaged in lipid nanoparticles. Antigen-presenting cells take up the nanoparticles and make the protein, which triggers an immune response. Example: mRNA vaccines against SARS-CoV-2.

cards.front: Complete: how CAR-T cells are made and given
cards.text: CAR-T cells are {{autologous}}: T cells are collected from the patient, transduced with a {{lentiviral}} vector, expanded, and infused back into the same patient after pre-treatment with {{cyclophosphamide}}.

cards.front: Short note: Gene therapy and antisense in drug development

points: Experimental approaches in new drug development, alongside antisense oligonucleotides (KDT8, preclinical stage)

cards.front: Which vector gives permanent expression by integrating into host DNA, and what is its drawback?
cards.back: Retroviruses integrate into host DNA and pass to daughter cells; the drawback is random insertion that can disrupt genes.

cards.front: How does a small interfering RNA (siRNA) silence a gene, and what is one clinical example?
cards.back: Short double-stranded RNA silences the complementary messenger RNA, so the protein is not made. Example: inclisiran, an siRNA against PCSK9, given twice yearly, reduces LDL-cholesterol by about 50%.

cards.front: Short note: CAR-T cell therapy

points: Patient's own T cells re-targeted with a chimeric antigen receptor
Receptor = antibody variable regions fused to T-cell signalling domains
A living drug
T cells purified from the patient's blood leukocytes
Transduced with a lentiviral (retroviral) vector, expanded, and infused back (autologous)
Cyclophosphamide pretreatment before infusion
CD19-directed products for B-cell leukaemias and lymphomas (tisagenlecleucel, axicabtagene, brexucabtagene, lisocabtagene)
BCMA-directed products for multiple myeloma (idecabtagene, ciltacabtagene)
Cytokine release syndrome: tocilizumab with or without corticosteroids
Neurotoxicity: supportive care
Prolonged hypogammaglobulinaemia: IGIV replacement
Resistance from loss of CD19 antigen

cards.front: How is cytokine release syndrome from CAR-T therapy treated?
cards.back: Tocilizumab (GG14 ch72).

cards.front: Short note: Current status of gene therapy

points: Addition of genetic material to cells to prevent, relieve or cure disease
Viral vectors replace a defective gene or add a new one; some approaches silence genes instead
AAV vectors deliver the RPE65 (retinal) and SMN1 (spinal muscular atrophy) genes
Anti-CD19 chimeric antigen receptor T cells, made with a lentiviral vector, treat B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukaemia
Patisiran and inotersen, transthyretin-directed RNA agents, treat hereditary transthyretin amyloidosis
Tisagenlecleucel (2017) was the first gene therapy approved in the United States
Tumour suppressor gene insertion, oncolytic virotherapy and gene-directed enzyme prodrug therapy are used for many cancers

cards.front: What is granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor (GM-CSF)?
cards.back: A haematopoietic cytokine that stimulates stem cells to differentiate into granulocytes (neutrophils, eosinophils, basophils) and monocytes. Recombinant sargramostim is used clinically to speed marrow recovery.

cards.front: Short note: Sargramostim

points: Recombinant human GM-CSF
Stimulates haematopoietic stem cells to become granulocytes and monocytes
Accelerates myeloid reconstitution after autologous bone marrow or peripheral blood progenitor cell transplant
Promotes neutrophil recovery after chemotherapy
Induces neutrophil production after myelosuppressive doses of radiation

cards.front: What is an immunotoxin?
cards.back: A targeting protein (an antibody fragment or a cytokine) coupled to a toxin, so the toxin reaches only cells carrying the target. Example: moxetumomab pasudotox-tdfk, an anti-CD22 Fv linked to a 38 kDa Pseudomonas toxin fragment.

cards.front: How does botulinum toxin block the neuromuscular junction?
cards.back: It binds cholinergic nerve endings, enters the cell and cleaves SNARE proteins (synaptobrevin), so ACh cannot be released. The result is flaccid paralysis; the block lasts several weeks to 3-4 months.

cards.front: Short note: Toxin-based drugs approved by USFDA

points: AbobotulinumtoxinA
IncobotulinumtoxinA
OnabotulinumtoxinA
PrabotulinumtoxinA-xvfs
RimabotulinumtoxinB
Mechanism: cleave SNARE proteins, block ACh release, flaccid paralysis
Moxetumomab pasudotox-tdfk: anti-CD22 Fv with Pseudomonas toxin fragment; refractory hairy cell leukaemia
Denileukin diftitox: named as an FDA-approved immunotoxin

cards.front: Alemtuzumab: target and effect in transplant induction?
cards.back: Anti-CD52 antibody. Mature lymphocytes express CD52, so binding depletes them, producing prolonged lymphocyte depletion; used as a depleting induction agent.

cards.front: Daclizumab and basiliximab: target and effect?
cards.back: Antibodies to the IL-2 receptor (CD25). They block IL-2 signalling, so activated T cells cannot proliferate. They modulate rather than deplete.

cards.front: Belatacept: which costimulatory ligands does it block?
cards.back: CD80 and CD86 on antigen-presenting cells. Blocking them inhibits T-cell costimulation without depleting cells.

cards.front: Muromonab-CD3: target and mechanism?
cards.back: It binds the CD3 chain next to the TCR, inducing its endocytosis and removal of the T cell, so helper T cells are depleted.

cards.front: Why was muromonab-CD3 largely replaced in transplant practice, and what happens if it is stopped?
cards.back: It is a murine antibody. Anaphylaxis, usual infections and neoplasms are risks, and stopping it can cause rebound rejection. Cytokine release syndrome and severe pulmonary oedema led to it being no longer marketed.

cards.front: Short note: Monoclonal antibodies in transplant rejection

points: Biological induction agents are of two types: depleting and immune modulating
ATG (lymphocyte immune globulin, Atgam; Thymoglobulin)
Muromonab-CD3, no longer marketed in the US
Alemtuzumab: CD52, depletes lymphocytes
Daclizumab and basiliximab: IL-2 receptor blockade
Belatacept: blocks CD80/CD86 costimulation
Rebound rejection after stopping muromonab-CD3

cards.front: What is chimeraplasty?
cards.back: A gene-editing method that uses a chimeric RNA-DNA oligonucleotide (a chimeraplast). It pairs with the target gene and carries the wanted base change, creating a mismatch that the cell's own repair machinery corrects. It changes one base or a small region of genomic DNA, and needs no viral vector.
refs: WEB Europe PMC Ranjbaran chimeraplast gene targeting 2018 https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC6004989

cards.front: Short note: Chimeraplasty

points: Gene repair using a chimeric RNA-DNA oligonucleotide (chimeraplast)
Aims at a point mutation or single-nucleotide change in genomic DNA
Chimeraplast pairs with the target sequence and carries the wanted base
The mismatch is recognised by the cell's own repair system, which converts the gene
Gene conversion about 7% in erythroid progenitor cells and 11% in K562 cells
Oligonucleotide-directed editing in plant protoplasts reached about 0.05%
Low and variable efficiency
Early high reports were not reproduced in later studies
Delivery into target cells remains a hurdle
Knockout: removes or disrupts the gene, often permanently
Antisense: binds mRNA and blocks the protein, transient effect
Chimeraplasty: changes the DNA sequence itself
